scenes.narration: Counting is a classic dictionary job. The keys are the things you count. The values are the counts. Think of a tally sheet. Each time you see a letter, you add one mark next to it. But a new letter has no mark yet. You must start it at zero, or one. The get method with a default zero does this in one line. And Python has a ready made helper called Counter.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: no starting value
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We try to add one to a count that does not exist yet. Python says, key error, g. The plus equals line reads the old count first, and a brand new letter has none. Use get with a default of zero, and the first time gives zero plus one. Then every later time just adds one more.

props.why: counts[ch] += 1 reads the key before it exists, which raises a KeyError; get with a default gives a starting value.

shorts.title: Counting with a dictionary
shorts.script: Counting is a classic dictionary job. The keys are the things you count. The values are the counts. Think of a tally sheet, where you add a mark for each letter you see. Loop over the text, and for each letter, add one to its count. At the end, the dictionary shows how many times each letter appeared. It is the base of every word counter. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: A tally sheet in code.

shorts.title: The if and else way
shorts.hook: "The simple way to count is with if and else."
shorts.script: The simple way to count is with if and else. If the letter is already a key, add one to its count. Otherwise, this is the first time, so set its count to one. It is clear and easy to read, and it works. Many beginners start here, and that is a perfectly good way to learn the idea. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: The clear way.

shorts.title: The get way
shorts.script: The shorter way uses get. Counts of ch equals counts dot get, ch, zero, plus one. Get returns the current count, or zero if the letter is new. Then we add one, and save it back. Two lines become one. You see this pattern in most real Python code. Learn to read it, and to write it. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: One line to count.

shorts.title: Key error on a new key
shorts.script: The bug. You write counts of ch, plus equals one, but the key does not exist yet. Python says, key error. The line tries to read the old count first, and a brand new letter has none. Use get with a default of zero, and the first time works. Every key needs a starting value before you add to it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Start at zero.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "Why did the dictionary count on everyone?"
shorts.script: Why did the dictionary count on everyone? It never lost track. Your challenge. Count how many times each letter appears in the word coconut. Use a dictionary and a loop. Print the final dictionary. You should see c twice, and o twice. Then try the Counter helper from the collections module, and check that you get the same answer. Share your result below. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 39.
shorts.caption: Try counting.

codeFiles.source:
from collections import Counter
text = "banana"
counts = {}
for ch in text:
    counts[ch] = counts.get(ch, 0) + 1
print(counts)
print(Counter(text).most_common(1))
